nameStory: The Mustached Clubtail gets its charming name from the distinctive pale yellow stripes that curve around its face like a handlebar mustache. Like all clubtails, it has a swollen tip at the end of its abdomen that resembles a club, giving the entire dragonfly family its common name.
description: The Mustached Clubtail is a medium-sized dragonfly with a slender black and yellow body that measures about 2-2.5 inches long. Its most striking feature is the pale yellow facial markings that look like a mustache, contrasting beautifully with its dark head. The body is primarily black with yellow stripes running down the thorax (middle section), and the abdomen ends in the characteristic clubbed shape. Unlike many dragonflies, clubtails typically rest on the ground or low perches rather than hovering constantly.

idTips.label: Mustache markings
idTips.description: Look for distinctive pale yellow curved stripes across the face that truly resemble a handlebar mustache - this marking is unique and unmistakable when viewed head-on

idTips.label: Ground-resting behavior
idTips.description: Unlike many dragonflies, clubtails prefer to rest directly on bare ground, rocks, or low surfaces where they feel warm and gritty to the touch if handled gently

idTips.label: Yellow thorax stripes
idTips.description: The middle body section shows bright yellow stripes against black background, creating a bold contrast that's visible even from several feet away

idTips.label: Clubbed abdomen tip
idTips.description: The tail end is noticeably swollen and bulbous compared to the slender abdomen shaft, giving it a club-like appearance that's obvious in profile

idTips.label: Clear wings with dark veins
idTips.description: Wings are completely transparent with dark black veining that creates a delicate lattice pattern, making a soft rustling sound when the dragonfly takes flight

habitat: Mustached Clubtails are found along clean, flowing streams and small rivers throughout New England's forested areas. They prefer rocky or sandy stream beds with moderate current and overhanging deciduous trees like maples and oaks. Look for them in areas where the water runs clear over gravel bottoms, especially in partially shaded spots where they can warm themselves on sun-heated rocks.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging from streams in late May, but are most easily spotted in early June when they're actively seeking mates and establishing territories.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity occurs from mid-June through July when adults are most abundant and easiest to observe perched along streambanks during warm, sunny afternoons.
seasonality.fall: By late August most adults have died off after mating, though larvae continue developing underwater and can sometimes be found under rocks in streams.
seasonality.winter: Only the aquatic larvae are present, buried in stream sediments where they'll spend 2-3 years developing before emerging as adults.

funFact: Mustached Clubtail larvae are incredible underwater predators that can shoot out their extendable lower jaw like a harpoon to catch prey - this lightning-fast jaw can extend nearly half the length of their body in just milliseconds, faster than a human eye can follow!
confusionNotes: The Mustached Clubtail is most easily confused with its close relative, the Spine-crowned Clubtail, but the mustache markings are the dead giveaway - remember 'mustache = Mustached' and look for those distinctive curved yellow facial stripes that the Spine-crowned lacks.
compareHints: Compared to the Spine-crowned Clubtail, the only other Hylogomphus species in New England, the Mustached Clubtail has those unmistakable yellow facial stripes while the Spine-crowned has spiny projections on the back of its head instead. Both species prefer similar stream habitats, but the Spine-crowned tends to favor slightly larger rivers with more open canopy.
